characters.description: General Yepanchin's forceful wife and mother of three daughters. She is impulsive, proud of her family, and intrigued by Myshkin's apparent innocence, partly because they share the Myshkin family name.
characters.name: Lizaveta Prokofyevna Yepanchina

characters.description: The youngest Yepanchin daughter. Intelligent, beautiful, and guarded behind teasing behavior, she is curious about Myshkin but resists being interpreted or managed by her family.
characters.name: Aglaya Yepanchina

characters.description: A wealthy landowner who became Nastasya Filippovna's guardian after her father's death and shaped her upbringing for his own benefit. He now wants to free himself for a respectable marriage and supports a financial arrangement intended to marry her to Ganya.
characters.name: Afanasiy Ivanovich Totsky

characters.description: Ganya's adolescent brother, friendly, direct, and less constrained by status than the adults around him. He takes quickly to Myshkin and becomes a dependable messenger and companion.
characters.name: Kolya Ivolgin

characters.description: Ganya and Kolya's father, a retired general who tells grandiose and frequently impossible stories about his past. His household treats his fabrications with weary familiarity, while Myshkin responds without humiliating him.
characters.name: General Ardalion Ivolgin

characters.description: A gravely ill young man in Kolya's circle who knows he has little time left. Proud, intellectually combative, and desperate to retain control over how others see him, he reacts sharply to pity and to Myshkin's compassion.
characters.name: Ippolit Terentyev

characters.description: A wealthy and polished young officer moving in the Yepanchins' social circle. He is regarded as a suitable match for Aglaya and observes Myshkin with a mixture of skepticism, intelligence, and growing sympathy.
characters.name: Evgeny Pavlovich Radomsky

recaps.ending: Aglaya arranges a meeting with Nastasya Filippovna, hoping to settle which woman Myshkin truly loves. Their confrontation becomes cruel and competitive. When Nastasya collapses, Myshkin turns to comfort her, and Aglaya leaves, understanding his choice as a rejection. Myshkin prepares to marry Nastasya, but she panics at the church and escapes with Rogozhin. Myshkin follows them to Saint Petersburg and finds Rogozhin in his darkened house beside Nastasya's murdered body. He stays with the delirious killer through the night, soothing him as his own mind fails. Rogozhin is later convicted and sent to Siberia. Myshkin returns to the Swiss clinic in a state from which recovery appears unlikely. Aglaya hastily marries a Polish émigré whose claims and political cause estrange her from her family. The Yepanchins visit Myshkin abroad, while Evgeny Pavlovich remains attentive to him. The attempt to save everyone has ended without rescuing Nastasya, Rogozhin, Aglaya, or the prince himself.
recaps.in_short: Prince Myshkin returns to Russia after treatment for epilepsy and enters a society driven by money, vanity, desire, and shame. His compassion draws him toward Nastasya Filippovna, who has been exploited by her guardian and alternates between seeking rescue and accepting others' condemnation. The wealthy, obsessive Rogozhin also pursues her. Myshkin unexpectedly inherits a fortune, but wealth does not make him socially adept or able to heal those around him. In Pavlovsk he grows close to Aglaya Yepanchina while remaining bound to Nastasya by pity and love. A confrontation between the two women forces the conflict into the open: Myshkin turns to Nastasya, losing Aglaya. Nastasya agrees to marry him but flees from the wedding with Rogozhin, who murders her. Myshkin finds them beside her body and relapses into profound illness; Rogozhin is sent to Siberia, and Aglaya makes an unhappy break with her family.

recaps.text: Prince Lev Myshkin returns to Russia after years in a Swiss clinic for epilepsy. On the train he meets Parfyon Rogozhin, newly enriched by an inheritance and passionately fixated on Nastasya Filippovna, and the inquisitive clerk Lebedev. In Saint Petersburg, Myshkin calls on his distant relation General Yepanchin despite having almost no money or prospects. His direct manner first seems naive, but his memories of Switzerland and his reflections on suffering hold the general's attention. Myshkin meets the secretary Ganya and sees a portrait of Nastasya, whose expression fascinates and troubles him. He learns that Ganya may marry her in return for a substantial payment, even though she has long been controlled by the wealthy Totsky and is also being pursued by Rogozhin.

Myshkin meets General Yepanchin's wife and daughters, including the proud youngest, Aglaya, and impresses them with his candor. Lodging with Ganya's family, he walks into a bitter conflict over Ganya's proposed marriage. Nastasya arrives without warning, followed by Rogozhin and a noisy group offering her one hundred thousand rubles. Ganya nearly strikes his sister during the humiliation, and Myshkin intervenes. At Nastasya's birthday gathering, she asks Myshkin whether she should marry Ganya and accepts his judgment that she should not. News then confirms that Myshkin has inherited a fortune, and he offers to marry her himself. Convinced that she would ruin him, Nastasya rejects his rescue, throws Rogozhin's money into a fire as a test for Ganya, and leaves with Rogozhin. Myshkin follows, beginning a destructive triangle among compassion, possession, and self-condemnation.

After months away, Myshkin returns to Saint Petersburg and visits Rogozhin's gloomy house. Their conversation reveals that Nastasya has repeatedly moved between them, promising herself to one and then fleeing toward the other. Myshkin insists that his feeling for her is compassion rather than rivalry, and the men exchange crosses in a gesture of brotherhood. Yet Myshkin senses Rogozhin watching him and later believes he is being followed. At a hotel stairway Rogozhin raises a knife against him, but Myshkin suffers an epileptic seizure before the blow lands, and Rogozhin runs away. Myshkin recovers in Pavlovsk among the Yepanchins and other acquaintances, but the emotional conflict has followed him there.

At Pavlovsk, a group led by Burdovsky publicly claims that Myshkin's former benefactor was Burdovsky's father and demands money as a moral debt. Their newspaper attack is based on false information, but Myshkin still offers assistance, frustrating both his defenders and his accusers. The dying Ippolit, one of the group, rejects being reduced to an object of pity. Social visits become increasingly volatile as Myshkin's generosity exposes the self-interest and embarrassment of nearly everyone present. Nastasya also reappears at the edge of the Yepanchins' circle, publicly meddling in Evgeny Pavlovich's affairs. Her behavior threatens Aglaya's reputation and makes Myshkin's continuing bond with her impossible for the family to ignore.

Ippolit gathers the company and reads a long statement about illness, death, and his refusal to submit quietly to a world he finds indifferent. He then attempts to shoot himself, but the pistol fails because the cap is missing, leaving everyone uncertain whether the failure was accidental. Myshkin continues meeting Aglaya, who is drawn to him but also mocks his humility and tests whether he can act with dignity. Their private understanding begins to look like a possible engagement. At the same time, Nastasya sends Aglaya letters urging her to marry Myshkin, as if she could arrange his salvation while excluding herself. Instead of resolving the triangle, the letters bind the two women more tightly to each other's fear and pride.

The Yepanchins begin treating Myshkin as Aglaya's likely suitor, though both young people resist stating the matter plainly. A formal gathering meant to introduce him to important acquaintances ends badly when anxiety and moral passion carry him into an excited speech; he breaks a valuable vase and then suffers a seizure. Aglaya does not abandon him, but her family worries that affection cannot overcome his illness and social vulnerability. Around them, the Ivolgin family deteriorates: General Ivolgin's lies and drinking culminate in a stroke and death. Aglaya finally arranges a direct meeting with Nastasya, intending to confront the woman whose letters and claim on Myshkin have overshadowed their relationship.

Aglaya and Nastasya meet with Myshkin and Rogozhin present. Their attempt at clarification becomes a contest of pride and suffering. Aglaya accuses Nastasya of performing her misery and controlling Myshkin; Nastasya retaliates by asserting that she can command him. When Nastasya collapses, Myshkin instinctively goes to her, and Aglaya leaves. He soon plans to marry Nastasya, but on the wedding day she becomes terrified and runs to Rogozhin, who takes her away. Myshkin tracks them to Saint Petersburg. Rogozhin leads him to Nastasya's body: he has killed her and hidden with her in his house. Myshkin remains beside Rogozhin through the night, comforting him as his own reason disintegrates. Rogozhin is sentenced to Siberia, while Myshkin returns to the Swiss clinic with little hope of recovery. Aglaya marries a Polish émigré and becomes estranged from her family, leaving the surviving circle scattered and chastened.

characters.description: A young Russian prince returning from years of treatment for epilepsy in Switzerland. Nearly penniless and inexperienced in society, he meets strangers with an openness that others mistake for foolishness. His sympathy and lack of calculation make him an unsettling presence among people accustomed to pride, suspicion, and social maneuvering.
characters.name: Prince Lev Nikolayevich Myshkin

characters.description: A dark, intense young merchant's son whom Myshkin meets on the train to St Petersburg. He is returning after inheriting a fortune and speaks with consuming passion about Nastasya Filippovna, for whom he is ready to spend recklessly.
characters.name: Parfyon Semyonovich Rogozhin

characters.description: A talkative, shabby official who questions Myshkin and Rogozhin during their train journey. Quick to collect useful information and attach himself to wealth or influence, he is comic, intrusive, and more observant than his manner first suggests.
characters.name: Lukyan Timofeyevich Lebedev

characters.description: A prosperous general and distant connection of Myshkin's family. Practical and socially ambitious, he receives the unexpected visitor cautiously while balancing business, his household, and a delicate marriage arrangement involving his secretary.
characters.name: General Ivan Fyodorovich Epanchin

characters.description: General Epanchin's capable but proud young secretary. His family needs money, and he is considering a financially advantageous marriage to Nastasya Filippovna despite his resentment of the bargain and his concern for his social standing.
characters.name: Gavril Ardalionovich Ivolgin

characters.description: A beautiful young woman known to Myshkin first through her portrait and through other people's anxious discussion of her future. Formerly under Totsky's control, she is at the center of a proposed marriage to Ganya and is widely judged by a society that also fears her independence.
characters.name: Nastasya Filippovna Barashkova

characters.description: General Epanchin's forceful, candid wife and Myshkin's distant relative. She is curious about the nearly forgotten prince, fiercely involved in her daughters' lives, and impatient with evasiveness or social pretension.
characters.name: Lizaveta Prokofyevna Epanchina

characters.description: The youngest Epanchin daughter, intelligent, proud, and closely watched as a desirable prospective bride. She responds to Myshkin's guilelessness with a mixture of curiosity, teasing, and resistance to the plans others imagine for her.
characters.name: Aglaya Ivanovna Epanchina

characters.description: The older man whose guardianship of the orphaned Nastasya Filippovna became exploitative. Wishing to make a respectable marriage elsewhere, he supports the plan to marry her to Ganya with a large payment attached.
characters.name: Afanasiy Ivanovich Totsky

characters.description: Ganya's good-hearted adolescent brother. Friendly and direct despite the strains within the Ivolgin household, he readily befriends Myshkin and moves between several of the novel's divided social circles.
characters.name: Nikolay Ardalionovich Ivolgin

characters.description: Ganya's father, a retired general whose grand claims and elaborate stories contrast with his diminished circumstances. His drinking and unreliability embarrass his family, though Myshkin treats him with patience.
characters.name: General Ardalion Alexandrovich Ivolgin

characters.description: Ganya's clear-sighted sister, protective of her mother and unwilling to flatter either her brother's ambitions or Nastasya Filippovna. She faces the household's humiliations with firmness and practical judgment.
characters.name: Varvara Ardalionovna Ivolgina

characters.description: A consumptive young man associated with Kolya and with the group that challenges Myshkin over an alleged moral debt. Fiercely intelligent and conscious that he may die soon, he rejects condescension and insists on speaking for himself.
characters.name: Ippolit Terentyev

characters.description: A former army officer, boxer, and would-be journalist who joins the visitors pressing a claim against Myshkin. His bluster and dubious schemes coexist with an impulsive desire to confess and to be thought honorable.
characters.name: Keller

characters.description: A wealthy, polished young officer moving in the Epanchins' Pavlovsk circle. He is treated as a plausible match for Aglaya and approaches Myshkin with outward courtesy, even when gossip and rivalry make their position awkward.
characters.name: Yevgeny Pavlovich Radomsky

recaps.ending: Aglaya forces a meeting with Nastasya Filippovna, hoping to settle which woman Myshkin truly loves. The encounter becomes a contest of pride and suffering. When Nastasya orders Myshkin to choose, his alarm at her distress overcomes everything else; Aglaya leaves, and her connection with him is broken. Myshkin prepares to marry Nastasya, but at the ceremony she panics and runs away with Rogozhin. Myshkin tracks them to St Petersburg and learns that Rogozhin has murdered her. He remains beside Rogozhin and the body through the night, soothing the delirious killer, and the shock destroys his recovered reason. Rogozhin is convicted and sent to Siberia. Myshkin returns to the Swiss clinic in a state from which his doctor expects no recovery. The Epanchin family later travels abroad; Aglaya marries a Polish man who misrepresents his status and draws her into political and religious causes, estranging her from her family. Lizaveta Prokofyevna visits the unresponsive Myshkin and grieves over the ruin of the people she tried to protect.
recaps.in_short: Prince Myshkin returns to Russia after treatment for epilepsy and enters a society governed by money, pride, and romantic rivalry. His compassion draws him toward the traumatized Nastasya Filippovna, while his growing attachment to Aglaya Epanchina offers the possibility of another life. Nastasya repeatedly turns to the possessive Rogozhin, then back toward Myshkin, convinced that she is unworthy of rescue. Myshkin's refusal to condemn anyone wins trust but cannot resolve the desires gathering around him. Aglaya eventually confronts Nastasya and leaves when Myshkin responds to Nastasya's anguish. On the day Myshkin is to marry Nastasya, she flees with Rogozhin; Rogozhin murders her. Myshkin finds them and keeps vigil with the killer beside her body, after which his mind collapses. On the train he meets Parfyon Rogozhin, newly enriched by an inheritance and passionately fixated on Nastasya Filippovna, and the inquisitive clerk Lebedev. In Saint Petersburg, Myshkin calls on his distant relation General Yepanchin despite having almost no money or prospects. His direct manner first seems naive, but his memories of Switzerland and his reflections on suffering hold the general's attention. Myshkin meets the secretary Ganya and sees a portrait of Nastasya, whose expression fascinates and troubles him. He learns that Ganya may marry her in return for a substantial payment, even though she has long been controlled by the wealthy Totsky and is also being pursued by Rogozhin.

Myshkin meets General Yepanchin's wife and daughters, including the proud youngest, Aglaya, and impresses them with his candor. Lodging with Ganya's family, he walks into a bitter conflict over Ganya's proposed marriage. Nastasya arrives without warning, followed by Rogozhin and a noisy group offering her one hundred thousand rubles. Ganya nearly strikes his sister during the humiliation, and Myshkin intervenes. At Nastasya's birthday gathering, she asks Myshkin whether she should marry Ganya and accepts his judgment that she should not. News then confirms that Myshkin has inherited a fortune, and he offers to marry her himself. Convinced that she would ruin him, Nastasya rejects his rescue, throws Rogozhin's money into a fire as a test for Ganya, and leaves with Rogozhin. Myshkin follows, beginning a destructive triangle among compassion, possession, and self-condemnation.

After months away, Myshkin returns to Saint Petersburg and visits Rogozhin's gloomy house. Their conversation reveals that Nastasya has repeatedly moved between them, promising herself to one and then fleeing toward the other. Myshkin insists that his feeling for her is compassion rather than rivalry, and the men exchange crosses in a gesture of brotherhood. Yet Myshkin senses Rogozhin watching him and later believes he is being followed. At a hotel stairway Rogozhin raises a knife against him, but Myshkin suffers an epileptic seizure before the blow lands, and Rogozhin runs away. Myshkin recovers in Pavlovsk among the Yepanchins and other acquaintances, but the emotional conflict has followed him there.

At Pavlovsk, a group led by Burdovsky publicly claims that Myshkin's former benefactor was Burdovsky's father and demands money as a moral debt. Their newspaper attack is based on false information, but Myshkin still offers assistance, frustrating both his defenders and his accusers. The dying Ippolit, one of the group, rejects being reduced to an object of pity. Social visits become increasingly volatile as Myshkin's generosity exposes the self-interest and embarrassment of nearly everyone present. Nastasya also reappears at the edge of the Yepanchins' circle, publicly meddling in Evgeny Pavlovich's affairs. Her behavior threatens Aglaya's reputation and makes Myshkin's continuing bond with her impossible for the family to ignore.

Ippolit gathers the company and reads a long statement about illness, death, and his refusal to submit quietly to a world he finds indifferent. He then attempts to shoot himself, but the pistol fails because the cap is missing, leaving everyone uncertain whether the failure was accidental. Myshkin continues meeting Aglaya, who is drawn to him but also mocks his humility and tests whether he can act with dignity. Their private understanding begins to look like a possible engagement. At the same time, Nastasya sends Aglaya letters urging her to marry Myshkin, as if she could arrange his salvation while excluding herself. Instead of resolving the triangle, the letters bind the two women more tightly to each other's fear and pride.

A formal gathering meant to introduce him to important acquaintances ends badly when anxiety and moral passion carry him into an excited speech; he breaks a valuable vase and then suffers a seizure. Aglaya does not abandon him, but her family worries that affection cannot overcome his illness and social vulnerability. Around them, the Ivolgin family deteriorates: General Ivolgin's lies and drinking culminate in a stroke and death. Aglaya finally arranges a direct meeting with Nastasya, intending to confront the woman whose letters and claim on Myshkin have overshadowed their relationship.

Aglaya accuses Nastasya of performing her misery and controlling Myshkin; Nastasya retaliates by asserting that she can command him. When Nastasya collapses, Myshkin instinctively goes to her, and Aglaya leaves. He soon plans to marry Nastasya, but on the wedding day she becomes terrified and runs to Rogozhin, who takes her away. Myshkin tracks them to Saint Petersburg. Rogozhin leads him to Nastasya's body: he has killed her and hidden with her in his house. Myshkin remains beside Rogozhin through the night, comforting him as his own reason disintegrates. Rogozhin is sentenced to Siberia, while Myshkin returns to the Swiss clinic with little hope of recovery. Aglaya marries a Polish émigré and becomes estranged from her family, leaving the surviving circle scattered and chastened.

He is considering marriage to Nastasya Filippovna in exchange for a large settlement, although desire, shame, and fear of public humiliation make him deeply divided about the arrangement.
characters.name: Gavril Ardalionovich Ivolgin

characters.description: A striking young woman raised and educated under the control of the wealthy Totsky after being orphaned on one of his estates. Petersburg society treats her as both scandalous and marriageable. Conscious of the exploitation behind her position, she alternates between proud defiance and a damaging belief that she deserves contempt.
characters.name: Nastasya Filippovna Barashkova

characters.description: General Yepanchin's outspoken wife and a distant member of the same princely family as Myshkin. Impulsive, suspicious of social maneuvering, and devoted to her three daughters, she is intrigued by the prince's simplicity and repeatedly draws him into the family's intimate affairs.
characters.name: Lizaveta Prokofyevna Yepanchina

characters.description: The youngest Yepanchin daughter, beautiful, intelligent, and restless beneath the expectations attached to an eligible society marriage. Her family regards her as the most striking and strong-willed of the three sisters.
characters.name: Aglaya Ivanovna Yepanchina

characters.description: Ganya's younger sister, practical and direct in a household strained by debt and her father's unreliability. She opposes a marriage that would bring money at the cost of family humiliation and is prepared to challenge her brother when ambition overrides affection.
characters.name: Varvara Ardalionovna Ivolgina

characters.description: Ganya's father, a retired general whose family lives with the consequences of his drinking and grandiose inventions. He tells elaborate stories of distinguished connections and past heroism, making it difficult to separate his genuine memories and need for respect from habitual falsehood.
characters.name: Ardalion Alexandrovich Ivolgin

characters.description: Ganya's adolescent brother, lively, independent-minded, and less burdened by social ambition than the adults around him. He quickly befriends Myshkin and moves easily between households, often carrying news or providing companionship when older characters withdraw into pride.
characters.name: Nikolay Ardalionovich Ivolgin

characters.description: A consumptive young man connected to Kolya and to the circle around Lebedev. Intellectually combative and painfully aware that he is dying, he resents pity and wants his final months to demonstrate complete independence. His arguments with Myshkin turn mortality into a public and personal challenge.
characters.name: Ippolit Terentyev

characters.description: A polished young man from the Yepanchins' social circle, wealthy, well connected, and regarded as a suitable possible husband for Aglaya. His ease and conventional social competence contrast with Myshkin's anxious sincerity.
characters.name: Yevgeny Pavlovich Radomsky

recaps.ending: Aglaya arranges a confrontation with Nastasya Filippovna, but the meeting becomes a contest of pride and suffering. When Nastasya collapses, Myshkin turns toward her, and Aglaya leaves, convinced she has lost him. Myshkin prepares to marry Nastasya, hoping love and care can free her from self-contempt. At the church, however, she flees with Rogozhin. Myshkin follows them to Petersburg and finds Rogozhin beside Nastasya's body after he has murdered her. The two men keep vigil through the night, with Myshkin comforting the killer as his own mind gives way. Rogozhin is later tried and sent to hard labor in Siberia. Myshkin's collapse is lasting, and he returns to the Swiss institution in essentially the same helpless condition as before his journey to Russia. Ippolit dies from his illness. The Yepanchins leave Russia; Aglaya becomes involved with a Polish émigré who deceives her and draws her away from her family and faith. Yevgeny Pavlovich remains concerned for Myshkin. The prince's compassion changes individual lives but cannot rescue Nastasya, cure Rogozhin's possessiveness, or survive the destructive claims placed upon it.
recaps.in_short: Prince Lev Myshkin returns to Russia after treatment for epilepsy and enters Petersburg society with an openness many mistake for stupidity. He becomes entangled with Nastasya Filippovna, a woman traumatized by exploitation and convinced she is ruined, and Rogozhin, whose love for her is possessive and violent. Myshkin's pity and love offer Nastasya another life, but she repeatedly flees him for Rogozhin. At the same time, Myshkin and the proud young Aglaya Yepanchina develop an unstable attachment shaped by idealization, embarrassment, and jealousy. Around them, families pursue money, status, and moral certainty, while the dying Ippolit challenges Myshkin's faith in compassion. Aglaya's confrontation with Nastasya destroys her bond with the prince. Nastasya agrees to marry Myshkin but escapes with Rogozhin at the wedding; Rogozhin murders her. Myshkin finds them and suffers a final mental collapse while comforting Rogozhin. He returns to institutional care, Rogozhin goes to Siberia, and Aglaya is drawn into an unhappy life abroad.

recaps.text: Prince Lev Myshkin returns to Russia after several years in a Swiss clinic, nearly penniless and still vulnerable to epileptic seizures. On the train he meets Parfyon Rogozhin, newly wealthy after his father's death, and Lebedev, a civil servant who knows Petersburg's scandals. Rogozhin describes his obsession with Nastasya Filippovna, a beautiful woman whose guardian Totsky exploited her and now wants to settle money on her so he can marry elsewhere. Myshkin calls on General Yepanchin, husband of his distant relative Lizaveta Prokofyevna, and impresses the family with his frankness and calligraphy. He also meets the general's secretary Ganya Ivolgin, who is considering marrying Nastasya for a large payment despite his shame about the bargain. A portrait of Nastasya affects Myshkin strongly. He takes a room with Ganya's strained family and is drawn at once into their conflict over the proposed marriage.

Nastasya arrives at the Ivolgins' home and deliberately exposes the family's resentments, while Rogozhin appears with a disorderly group and offers an enormous sum for her. Ganya's humiliation leads him to raise a hand against his sister Varya; Myshkin intervenes and receives the blow instead. At Nastasya's birthday gathering, she asks Myshkin whether she should marry Ganya and accepts his judgment that she should not. Myshkin then offers to marry her himself, insisting that she is not defined by what Totsky did to her. News of a possible inheritance makes his proposal financially credible. Nastasya is moved but cannot believe herself fit for the life he imagines. She subjects Ganya to a final test involving Rogozhin's money, rejects the respectable settlement, and leaves with Rogozhin. Myshkin follows, not as a rival seeking possession but because he fears what their destructive passion will produce.

After several months away, Myshkin has received a substantial inheritance and attempted to settle numerous claims upon it. His relations with Nastasya and Rogozhin have become a repeated cycle: Nastasya approaches marriage with one man, then flees toward the other, while Rogozhin's jealousy darkens into violence. Back in Petersburg, Myshkin visits Rogozhin's shadowed house. They exchange crosses and speak like brothers, yet Myshkin senses that Rogozhin may kill either Nastasya or him. Later Rogozhin follows the prince and raises a knife, but Myshkin suffers a seizure at the instant of attack and survives. He recovers in Pavlovsk among Lebedev, Kolya, and the Yepanchin family. A group of young men, including Burdovsky and the dying Ippolit, publicly demand part of Myshkin's fortune through a false claim about his benefactor. Although their case is discredited, Myshkin responds with generosity that embarrasses allies who wanted him to defend himself more firmly.

Life in Pavlovsk brings Myshkin repeatedly into the Yepanchins' circle, where his connection with Aglaya becomes the subject of family hope, mockery, and confusion. Aglaya is attracted to his moral seriousness but resents being treated as an innocent girl or as a cure for his concern with Nastasya. She tests him through teasing, secret meetings, and allusions to an idealized knight, while Yevgeny Pavlovich appears as a socially conventional alternative. Nastasya remains nearby and intervenes publicly in the Yepanchins' affairs, apparently trying to arrange Aglaya's future while also making herself impossible to forget. During a gathering for Myshkin's birthday, Ippolit reads a long statement about illness, isolation, and his refusal to submit meekly to death. He then tries to shoot himself, but the weapon fails to fire. The guests dispute whether the failure was deliberate, leaving Ippolit alive and humiliated in the face of the pity he rejects.

Aglaya's family increasingly treats her attachment to Myshkin as a possible engagement, though neither she nor the prince can state a stable understanding of what they want. Myshkin loves Aglaya, but his enduring compassion for Nastasya is inseparable from dread that she will be destroyed. At a formal gathering intended to introduce him to influential society, he becomes overexcited, breaks a valuable vase he had been warned about, launches into an earnest speech, and suffers another seizure. The Yepanchins are embarrassed, yet Aglaya continues to seek clarity from him. Nastasya's presence makes that impossible. Aglaya finally decides to meet her directly, hoping to force a choice and to determine whether Myshkin's bond with Nastasya is love, pity, or a form of mutual idealization. Every participant approaches the confrontation with a different hope, and Myshkin lacks the emotional boundaries needed to protect either woman from the other.

Aglaya confronts Nastasya, but their conversation turns cruel as each attacks the other's claim upon Myshkin. When Nastasya breaks down, Myshkin instinctively goes to her. Aglaya leaves, and the possibility of their marriage collapses. Myshkin now prepares to marry Nastasya, who briefly believes his devotion may make a new life possible. At the wedding itself she panics and runs to Rogozhin, who takes her away. Myshkin tracks them to Petersburg and finds Rogozhin in his house beside Nastasya's murdered body. Rogozhin has killed the woman he could neither trust nor release. Myshkin remains with him through the night, responding to horror with helpless tenderness until his own reason collapses. Rogozhin is convicted and sent to Siberian hard labor. Myshkin returns to the Swiss clinic with little prospect of recovery. Ippolit dies, and the Yepanchins travel abroad, where Aglaya falls under the influence of a deceptive Polish émigré and becomes estranged from her family. Myshkin's radical compassion has exposed the people around him but has not saved Nastasya, Rogozhin, Aglaya, or himself.

characters.description: The greatest warrior in the Greek army at Troy, renowned for speed and unmatched combat skill. Proud and intensely conscious of honor, he withdraws from battle after Agamemnon publicly takes the captive woman awarded to him, making their dispute the central crisis of the Greek campaign.
characters.name: Achilles

characters.description: King of Mycenae and commander of the assembled Greek forces at Troy. His refusal to yield a captive woman brings divine punishment on the army, and his later decision to take Achilles' prize turns a dispute over authority into a dangerous division among the Greeks.
characters.name: Agamemnon

characters.description: Achilles' closest companion and trusted member of his household. He remains with Achilles when their contingent withdraws from the fighting and carries out his friend's instructions.
characters.name: Patroclus

characters.description: The sea goddess and mother of Achilles. She hears his grief after Agamemnon dishonors him and agrees to ask Zeus to let the Greeks suffer until they recognize her son's importance.
characters.name: Thetis

characters.description: Goddess of wisdom, strategy, and disciplined warfare. She supports the Greeks at Troy and restrains Achilles from killing Agamemnon during their quarrel, imposing divine control before his anger becomes murder.
characters.name: Athena

characters.description: Ruler of the gods, whose decisions shape the balance of the Trojan War. He agrees to honor Achilles by allowing Trojan success, even though other gods have their own loyalties in the conflict.
characters.name: Zeus

characters.description: King of Ithaca, a leading Greek commander at Troy, and a persuasive speaker known for intelligence and self-control. He helps maintain order during the dispute in the army and undertakes difficult missions requiring judgment as well as courage.
characters.name: Odysseus

characters.description: The foremost Trojan warrior, eldest son of Priam, and defender of his city. He fights from duty to Troy and his family, providing a disciplined counterpart to the divided Greek champions.
characters.name: Hector

characters.description: A Trojan prince whose taking of Helen from Menelaus caused the war. Handsome but unreliable in battle, he accepts a duel with Menelaus that offers a possible end to the conflict.
characters.name: Paris

characters.description: Wife of Menelaus, now living in Troy with Paris, whose departure with him stands at the origin of the war. She regrets the destruction associated with her choice and identifies the Greek commanders for Priam from the city wall.
characters.name: Helen

characters.description: The elderly king of Troy and father of Hector and Paris. Courteous even toward Helen and painfully aware of the cost of the war, he presides over a royal family whose fate is bound to the city's defense.
characters.name: Priam

characters.description: Hector's wife and the mother of their young son. Having already lost her birth family to war, she begs Hector to preserve himself, while he believes honor and duty require him to return to the defense of Troy.
characters.name: Andromache

characters.description: The young son of Odysseus and Penelope, now nearing adulthood while disorder grows in his father's house. Athena urges him to challenge the suitors consuming his inheritance and to seek reliable news of Odysseus.
characters.name: Telemachus

characters.description: Odysseus' faithful wife and queen of Ithaca. Besieged by men demanding that she choose a new husband, she delays them while grieving for Odysseus and trying to protect her household and son.
characters.name: Penelope

characters.description: The most aggressive of Penelope's suitors. Arrogant and wasteful, he dominates the men occupying Odysseus' palace and resents any challenge from Telemachus.
characters.name: Antinous

characters.description: A goddess who has kept Odysseus on her remote island for years and wants him as her husband. Though she offers comfort and immortality, her love prevents him from returning to the mortal home he longs for.
characters.name: Calypso

characters.description: A Phaeacian princess who encounters the shipwrecked Odysseus while washing clothes with her attendants. She responds to the stranger with courage and hospitality and explains how he can seek help from her parents.
characters.name: Nausicaa

characters.description: A one-eyed Cyclops and son of Poseidon who traps Odysseus and his crew inside his cave. Immensely strong and contemptuous of hospitality, he treats the stranded sailors as prey.
characters.name: Polyphemus

characters.description: A powerful enchantress living on Aeaea. She transforms members of Odysseus' crew into swine, but Odysseus approaches her protected by divine help and demands their restoration.
characters.name: Circe

characters.description: Odysseus' loyal swineherd in Ithaca. Though living modestly and believing his master may never return, he protects the estate's animals as best he can and offers generous hospitality to a stranger.
characters.name: Eumaeus

recaps.ending: The Iliad closes before Troy falls. Achilles kills Hector, but Priam enters the Greek camp and persuades him to return his son's body. Their shared grief briefly crosses the boundary between enemies, and the Trojans mourn and bury Hector. The Odyssey ends the larger homecoming story. Odysseus returns to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, reveals himself to Telemachus and a few loyal servants, and wins Penelope's bow contest. He and his allies kill the suitors occupying his house. Penelope tests the stranger with private knowledge of their immovable marriage bed and accepts that Odysseus has truly returned. He then reunites with his father Laertes. When the suitors' relatives seek vengeance, Athena intervenes under Zeus's authority and imposes peace, restoring Odysseus to his family and kingdom.
recaps.in_short: The Iliad follows a crisis late in the Trojan War: Achilles withdraws after Agamemnon insults him, and the Greeks suffer without their greatest warrior. Achilles' companion Patroclus enters battle in his armor and is killed by Hector. Grief drives Achilles back to war; he kills Hector and abuses the body, but finally returns it when King Priam appeals to him as a grieving father. The epic ends with Hector's funeral. The Odyssey follows Odysseus' return from Troy. After years detained by Calypso, he reaches the Phaeacians and recounts the Cyclops, Circe, the underworld, the Sirens, and the loss of his crew. Back in Ithaca, Athena disguises him while he joins Telemachus against the suitors occupying his palace. Odysseus wins a bow contest, kills the suitors with loyal allies, proves his identity to Penelope, reunites with his father, and regains his household when Athena ends the threat of further revenge.

recaps.text: Late in the Greek siege of Troy, Apollo sends a plague after Agamemnon refuses to return a captive woman to her priestly father. Agamemnon yields only after demanding Briseis, the woman awarded to Achilles. Enraged by the public humiliation, Achilles withdraws himself and his troops and asks his divine mother Thetis to make the Greeks recognize what they have lost. Zeus permits Trojan success. A proposed truce fails when Paris' duel with Menelaus does not settle the war, and fighting resumes under the influence of competing gods. Diomedes leads a fierce Greek advance, while Hector returns to Troy, meets Helen and Paris, and takes leave of his wife Andromache and their son before returning to battle.

Hector and Ajax fight to a draw, and the armies pause to bury their dead. Zeus then forbids the gods from intervening and allows the Trojans to drive the Greeks back behind their fortifications. Faced with disaster, Agamemnon admits his offense and sends Odysseus, Ajax, and Phoenix to offer Achilles wealth, honor, and the return of Briseis. Achilles rejects the embassy, still valuing his wounded honor above the campaign. Greek scouts Odysseus and Diomedes raid the Trojan side at night, but daylight brings renewed losses: Agamemnon and other major Greek fighters are wounded. The Trojans break through the wall and threaten the ships, while Patroclus begins to see how desperate the situation has become.

The battle reaches the Greek ships. Patroclus begs Achilles to let him enter combat wearing Achilles' armor, hoping the sight will frighten the Trojans away. Achilles agrees but orders him to save the ships and return. Patroclus leads the Myrmidons, drives the Trojans back, and kills Sarpedon, a son of Zeus. Carried beyond his intended mission by success, he advances to Troy's walls. Apollo weakens and disarms him, and Hector kills him. Greeks and Trojans struggle over Patroclus' body while Hector takes Achilles' armor. When Achilles learns of his companion's death, his anger gives way to devastating grief. Thetis promises new armor from Hephaestus, and Achilles appears at the defenses long enough to terrify the Trojans and protect the recovery of Patroclus' body.

Reconciled with Agamemnon but fixed on revenge, Achilles returns to battle in armor forged by Hephaestus. He drives the Trojans toward the city, fights even the river that rises against his slaughter, and meets Hector outside the walls. Hector first flees, then stands and is killed. Achilles drags the body behind his chariot and continues to mourn Patroclus, whose funeral includes games among the Greek leaders. The gods preserve Hector's body and condemn its abuse. Guided by the gods, the aged Priam enters Achilles' shelter, kneels before the killer of his son, and asks for the body back. Remembering his own father and sharing Priam's grief, Achilles relents and grants time for mourning. The Trojans lament Hector and bury him; the poem ends with his funeral, not the capture of Troy.

Years after Troy, Odysseus is still absent from Ithaca. Suitors occupy his palace, consume his wealth, and pressure Penelope to remarry. Athena, disguised as family friends, urges Telemachus to seek news of his father. He calls an assembly, then visits Nestor at Pylos and Menelaus and Helen at Sparta, learning that Odysseus is alive but detained by Calypso. The suitors plan to ambush Telemachus on his return. Meanwhile Zeus orders Calypso to release Odysseus. He builds a raft, but Poseidon wrecks it; after a long struggle he reaches the land of the Phaeacians alone and exhausted.

Nausicaa helps the shipwrecked Odysseus approach the Phaeacian court, where King Alcinous promises passage home. Odysseus reveals his identity and recounts the journey that followed Troy. His men raid the Cicones, encounter the Lotus-Eaters, and are trapped by the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus blinds the monster and escapes beneath sheep, but his boast allows Polyphemus to ask Poseidon for vengeance. Aeolus gives Odysseus the winds needed to reach home, yet the crew opens the bag and is blown away again. Cannibal Laestrygonians destroy all ships but Odysseus' own. On Aeaea, Circe turns part of the crew into swine; protected by Hermes, Odysseus makes her restore them, and the company remains with her for a year.

Following Circe's instructions, Odysseus consults the dead and learns from Tiresias how he may reach home. He also encounters his mother and fallen heroes. The crew returns to sea, passes the Sirens and the deadly passage between Scylla and Charybdis, then lands where the sun god's cattle must not be harmed. While Odysseus sleeps, his starving men kill the cattle. Zeus destroys their ship, leaving Odysseus the sole survivor; after further suffering he reaches Calypso's island, completing the account he tells the Phaeacians. They carry him sleeping to Ithaca. Athena disguises him as a beggar, and he finds the loyal swineherd Eumaeus. Telemachus escapes the suitors' ambush and joins them. Odysseus reveals himself to his son, and they begin planning to clear the palace.

Telemachus returns openly to the palace while Odysseus enters in disguise with Eumaeus. The old dog Argos recognizes his master and dies. Antinous strikes the supposed beggar, and the other suitors continue abusing the household's hospitality. Penelope questions the stranger, who gives her a carefully disguised account and assures her that Odysseus is near. The nurse Eurycleia recognizes a scar while washing his feet, but he makes her keep silent. Athena helps Odysseus endure further insults and assess allies and enemies. Penelope announces a contest: she will marry the man who can string Odysseus' bow and shoot through a row of axe heads. Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus, and the loyal cowherd Philoetius prepare to trap the suitors inside.

The suitors cannot string Odysseus' bow. Still disguised, Odysseus takes it, completes the shot, and then reveals himself. With Telemachus, Eumaeus, Philoetius, and Athena's support, he kills Antinous and the other suitors, despite their attempts to bargain or fight back. Disloyal servants are punished, and Eurycleia tells Penelope that her husband has returned. Penelope remains cautious until she tests him by referring to moving their marriage bed; Odysseus' knowledge that he built it around a living olive tree proves his identity. They reunite and exchange their stories. Odysseus then visits his father Laertes and proves himself again. Relatives of the dead suitors gather for revenge, but Zeus and Athena require the conflict to end. Athena imposes peace, leaving Odysseus restored to his wife, son, father, household, and rule in Ithaca.

characters.description: A respectable country guardian who uses the name Ernest during visits to London. He has invented a troublesome brother as an excuse to leave his responsibilities and hopes to marry Gwendolen, whose attachment to the name Ernest complicates his proposal.
characters.name: Jack Worthing

characters.description: Jack's witty and idle friend, a London bachelor who escapes unwanted engagements by visiting an imaginary invalid named Bunbury. Curious about Jack's double life, he treats deception as an art and is quick to exploit what he learns.
characters.name: Algernon Moncrieff

characters.description: Algernon's poised cousin and the woman Jack wants to marry. She returns Jack's affection but insists that she could only truly love a man named Ernest, making his assumed identity central to their courtship.
characters.name: Gwendolen Fairfax

characters.description: Gwendolen's formidable mother and Algernon's aunt. She evaluates marriage as a matter of family, wealth, and social position, questioning Jack closely and rejecting his proposal when his uncertain parentage fails her standards.
characters.name: Lady Bracknell

characters.description: Algernon's dry, capable manservant. He manages the household during the opening tea and answers his employer's questions with a reserve that hints at his own practical view of marriage and domestic life.
characters.name: Lane

characters.description: Jack's eighteen-year-old ward, raised at his country estate. Imaginative and self-possessed, she has already constructed a romantic history around Jack's supposedly wicked brother Ernest before meeting the visitor who claims that name.
characters.name: Cecily Cardew

characters.description: Cecily's learned governess, given to improving instruction and moral judgments. She has written an unpublished novel and shares a restrained mutual interest with the local clergyman, Canon Chasuble.
characters.name: Miss Prism

characters.description: The rector near Jack's country home. He is fond of Miss Prism and readily agrees to Jack's request for a christening, unaware that the ceremony is meant to make Jack's invented identity real.
characters.name: Reverend Chasuble

characters.description: The butler at Jack's country house. He announces visitors and serves refreshments while maintaining formal calm through the household's escalating romantic and social confusion.
characters.name: Merriman

recaps.ending: Miss Prism admits that, while working as a nurse years earlier, she accidentally put the infant in her handbag and her manuscript in the baby's carriage, then left the handbag at Victoria Station. Jack produces the same bag and embraces her as the person who lost him, but Lady Bracknell clarifies that he is actually the elder son of her late sister and therefore Algernon's brother. The army records show that Jack was named after his father, Ernest John Moncrieff, so his London name has unknowingly been his real name all along. His birth now satisfies Lady Bracknell's objection, allowing him to marry Gwendolen. Algernon and Cecily remain engaged, and Chasuble and Miss Prism also form a pair. Jack ends with a new appreciation of how much his real name matters.
recaps.in_short: Jack Worthing maintains a sober life as guardian to Cecily in the country and a second identity as Ernest in London, where he courts Gwendolen Fairfax. His friend Algernon discovers the deception, visits Cecily while pretending to be Jack's imaginary brother Ernest, and falls in love with her. Both women believe they are engaged to a man named Ernest, and the men's lies collapse when Gwendolen and Cecily meet. Lady Bracknell blocks Jack's marriage because he was found as a baby in a handbag, then approves wealthy Cecily for Algernon. Miss Prism finally reveals that she misplaced a baby years ago; the handbag proves Jack is Lady Bracknell's nephew, Algernon's elder brother, and the son of a man named Ernest. Jack's assumed name is thus his real one, clearing the way for the two young couples, while Miss Prism and Chasuble are also united.

recaps.text: In Algernon Moncrieff's London flat, his friend Ernest is exposed as Jack Worthing, a country gentleman who invented a disreputable brother named Ernest so he could escape to town under that identity. Algernon admits a similar device: an imaginary invalid friend, Bunbury, whose illnesses excuse him from social duties. Jack proposes to Algernon's cousin Gwendolen, who accepts but says the name Ernest is essential to her attraction. Her mother, Lady Bracknell, interrogates Jack and rejects him because he cannot identify his parents: he was found as a baby in a handbag at Victoria Station. Algernon secretly notes the address of Jack's country estate, where Jack's young ward Cecily lives. Jack intends to end his double life, but Algernon has gained the means to enter it.

At Jack's country house, Cecily studies with Miss Prism and has built an elaborate fantasy around her guardian's supposedly wicked brother Ernest. Algernon arrives pretending to be Ernest, and Cecily quickly accepts his proposal; she explains that in her private imagination they have effectively been engaged for months and that she, like Gwendolen, prizes the name Ernest. Jack returns in mourning and announces that his invented brother has died, only to find the supposed Ernest in his home. Both men separately ask Canon Chasuble to christen them Ernest. Gwendolen then arrives and meets Cecily. Their courteous rivalry turns openly hostile when each claims to be engaged to Ernest Worthing. Jack and Algernon enter together, exposing that neither man is Ernest. The women withdraw in solidarity while the two men blame each other for the collapse of their deceptions.

Jack and Algernon persuade Gwendolen and Cecily that their deceptions were motivated by love, and both men announce plans to be christened Ernest. Lady Bracknell arrives, still refusing Jack but rapidly approving Cecily as Algernon's bride after learning of her fortune. Jack, as Cecily's guardian, withholds consent unless Lady Bracknell permits his marriage to Gwendolen. The appearance of Miss Prism unlocks Jack's history: as a nurse, she accidentally placed her infant charge in a handbag and abandoned it at Victoria Station. Jack produces the bag in which he was found. Lady Bracknell identifies him as the lost elder son of her sister and therefore Algernon's brother. Records reveal that Jack was named for his father, Ernest John Moncrieff, making Ernest his true name. The objections dissolve; Jack and Gwendolen, Algernon and Cecily, and Miss Prism and Chasuble are paired at the close.

characters.description: A poor villager who discovers an ancient winged man lying helpless in the mud behind his house after days of rain. He and his wife confine the stranger in their chicken coop while deciding what the discovery may be worth.
characters.name: Pelayo

characters.description: Pelayo's wife, who quickly turns public curiosity about the winged captive into admission money. The resulting income transforms her family's circumstances, even as the old man remains neglected in their yard.
characters.name: Elisenda

characters.description: An extremely old, filthy, nearly toothless man with enormous wings who appears in Pelayo's courtyard. He speaks in an unknown language, endures confinement and gawking crowds with little resistance, and never fits the explanations imposed on him.
characters.name: The Old Man with Wings

characters.description: The village priest who examines the winged man and warns the crowd that wings alone do not prove holiness. He writes to church authorities for guidance while the public's fascination moves faster than any official judgment.
characters.name: Father Gonzaga

characters.description: A drowned stranger whose extraordinarily large and beautiful body washes up beside an isolated seaside village. The women preparing him for burial imagine the life he might have led and name him Esteban, and their response changes how the whole village sees itself.
characters.name: Esteban

characters.description: An ambitious senator campaigning for reelection despite knowing that he is terminally ill. His practiced promises and public spectacle are interrupted when he becomes fascinated by a young woman sent to ask him for a favor.
characters.name: Onésimo Sánchez

characters.description: The daughter of an outlaw living in the desert settlement where Senator Sánchez campaigns. Her father sends her to secure official help, but her encounter with the senator develops beyond the transaction planned for her.
characters.name: Laura Farina

characters.description: A cruel traveling showman who claims miraculous powers and makes a living through staged wonders, salesmanship, and intimidation. He takes on a younger assistant whom he exploits and publicly humiliates.
characters.name: Blacamán the Bad

characters.description: The abused apprentice and narrator of Blacamán's story. After suffering under the older performer's control, he discovers that his own healing power is genuine and begins to reverse their positions.
characters.name: Blacamán the Good

characters.description: A fourteen-year-old girl exhausted by endless domestic service to her grandmother in their isolated desert mansion. After an accidental fire destroys the house, her grandmother declares her responsible for the loss and forces her to work off an impossible debt.
characters.name: Innocent Eréndira

characters.description: Eréndira's immense, domineering grandmother, who treats the girl's labor and body as assets under her control. She turns their wandering household into a profitable business and continually recalculates the invented debt that keeps Eréndira captive.
characters.name: Eréndira's Grandmother

characters.description: A sheltered young man from a prosperous family of orange growers. He becomes devoted to Eréndira after meeting her at her grandmother's traveling tent and tries to help her escape despite the grandmother's vigilance.
characters.name: Ulises

recaps.ending: Ulises returns to Eréndira and makes repeated attempts to kill her grandmother. Poison and an explosion fail, but he finally attacks the old woman with a knife and kills her after a prolonged struggle. Instead of joining him, Eréndira takes the grandmother's vest filled with gold and runs alone into the desert. Ulises, bloodied and exhausted, calls after her but cannot follow. She disappears beyond the horizon and is never seen again. The grandmother's control is broken, yet the story does not turn the escape into a shared romantic future: Eréndira claims the portable wealth produced by her exploitation and leaves both her abuser and would-be rescuer behind.
recaps.in_short: Seven stories place the marvelous beside hardship without separating one from the other. An aged winged man becomes a profitable attraction before recovering and flying away; a coastal village remakes itself after adopting a magnificent drowned stranger as one of its own; and a dying senator's affair with Laura Farina becomes the scandal attached to his final months. Other narrators confront a phantom ship and a fraudulent miracle worker whose abused apprentice develops real power. In the title tale, fourteen-year-old Eréndira accidentally burns down her grandmother's mansion and is forced into sexual exploitation to repay an endlessly inflated debt. She falls in love with Ulises, who helps her escape but cannot initially free her from the grandmother. After his poison and explosives fail, he kills the old woman with a knife. Eréndira takes the grandmother's gold and runs away alone, leaving Ulises behind.

recaps.text: After heavy rain, Pelayo finds a decrepit old man with enormous wings collapsed in his courtyard. He and Elisenda shut the stranger in a chicken coop, and villagers arrive with competing theories about what he is. Father Gonzaga doubts that the captive is an angel and seeks guidance from church authorities, but the crowd treats him as a source of cures and entertainment. Pelayo and Elisenda charge admission and become wealthy. Public interest shifts to a more understandable traveling marvel, leaving the old man neglected. Years later his feathers recover; he struggles into the air and flies away while Elisenda watches him vanish. The next story moves to a coastal settlement where an uncanny scent from the sea briefly revives hopes and memories among residents accustomed to disappointment, then recedes without permanently changing their material lives.

Children discover the body of an unknown drowned man on the shore of a tiny village. As the women clean the exceptionally large and handsome corpse, they imagine the difficulties and generosity of his life and give him the name Esteban. The men confirm that he belongs to no neighboring community. By the time the village gives him an elaborate burial at sea, everyone has claimed kinship with him. They resolve to widen their doors, strengthen their houses, and plant flowers so their home will be worthy of his memory. In the next story, Senator Onésimo Sánchez campaigns through a desert town while secretly counting down the months left before his predicted death. He falls in love with Laura Farina, whose father sent her to obtain a favor. Their relationship becomes public, and the senator dies on schedule with the scandal and Laura's presence defining his last days.

A boy repeatedly sees a vast ocean liner passing where no ship can be, but the adults mock his reports. Determined to prove the apparition, he guides the ghost ship toward land with a light. The enormous vessel enters the village and establishes the truth of the vision through its catastrophic arrival. In the following story, Blacamán the Bad travels as a false healer, staging wonders and abusing the boy he has taken as an assistant. The apprentice eventually discovers a genuine ability to restore the dead. Renaming himself Blacamán the Good, he uses his gift to prosper and turns on his former master. He revives the older man only to keep him confined in a tomb where repeated death and restoration become punishment for the cruelty once inflicted on him.

Fourteen-year-old Eréndira serves her grandmother without rest in a desert mansion. After she falls asleep and a candle sets the house ablaze, the grandmother makes her responsible for the entire imagined value of the loss. She sells Eréndira's sexual services and carries her from town to town, growing rich while continually extending the debt. Missionaries temporarily remove the girl, but the grandmother recovers control. Ulises, the son of orange growers, falls in love with Eréndira and helps her flee; the grandmother tracks them down and takes her back. At Eréndira's urging, Ulises tries poison and then explosives, but the old woman survives both. He finally kills her with a knife. Eréndira seizes the vest holding the grandmother's gold and runs into the desert alone. She does not wait for Ulises, who is too injured to pursue her, and she disappears beyond reach.

characters.description: A suburban husband and father whose body begins losing a small, measurable amount of height each day after two unusual chemical exposures. Scott initially treats the change as a medical problem that can be solved, but the steady loss of size threatens his work, privacy, marriage, and sense of himself. The novel follows both his public decline and his later struggle to survive in an ordinary house transformed by scale.
characters.name: Scott Carey

characters.description: Scott's wife, confronted with a condition neither of them understands and with the practical burdens created as he becomes smaller. She tries to support him while his fear, anger, and increasing dependence place their marriage under severe strain.
characters.name: Louise Carey

characters.description: Scott and Louise's young daughter. As Scott diminishes, his changing relationship to Beth makes the loss of his familiar place within the family painfully visible.
characters.name: Beth Carey

characters.description: Scott's brother, who helps the Carey family deal with the practical and financial consequences of Scott's condition, including the unwanted public attention it attracts.
characters.name: Charlie Carey

characters.description: A physician involved in investigating Scott's unprecedented loss of height. He searches for a biological explanation and a treatment while being careful not to promise that medicine can reverse the process.
characters.name: Doctor Silver

characters.description: A very short woman Scott meets while his shrinking has made ordinary social encounters humiliating. Her ease with her own body offers him a brief experience of companionship without the same imbalance of scale.
characters.name: Clarice

characters.description: A large spider inhabiting the basement where Scott is stranded. At Scott's reduced scale it is a powerful predator and the chief obstacle between him and the food he needs to survive.
characters.name: The Spider

recaps.ending: Alone in the basement and now tiny enough for its boards, tools, and insects to form an alien landscape, Scott secures water and scraps of food while preparing to confront the spider that controls access to the remaining cake. He fashions weapons and climbing equipment from household debris and finally kills the spider after a dangerous struggle. His victory does not stop his body from diminishing. Scott finds a way through the basement screen and enters the outside world, expecting that reaching zero size will mean death. Instead, he passes beyond the scale visible to ordinary human beings and remains alive. Looking up at a universe that no longer fits his old measurements, he understands that smallness has no final boundary and that existence continues at scales his former life could not perceive. He moves forward into that unknown rather than treating himself as nothing.
recaps.in_short: After exposure to a strange mist and an insecticide, Scott Carey begins shrinking by a fixed fraction of an inch each day. Doctors cannot provide a lasting cure, and the change strips away his privacy, livelihood, confidence, and equal footing within his family. Public curiosity turns him into a spectacle, while his marriage to Louise buckles under fear and resentment. Once only inches tall, Scott is separated from his family and believed dead, but he is actually trapped in the basement. There he learns to obtain water and crumbs, crosses enormous distances through familiar household space, and fights a spider for access to food. He kills it, escapes through a screen, and continues shrinking past the point he had assumed would erase him. The world opens into another scale, and Scott accepts that there may be no absolute smallest size and no simple boundary at which his life must cease.

recaps.text: Scott Carey notices that his clothes fit differently and careful measurements confirm that he is becoming shorter. He and Louise first hope for an ordinary explanation, but the loss continues at a regular rate. Medical questioning identifies two events that may have acted together: Scott passed through an unusual mist while on a boat and was later exposed to insecticide. The condition is not merely cosmetic. Scott realizes that, unless it can be stopped, every part of his domestic and working life will change. Doctors begin tests while he and Louise try to keep the problem private.

Scott's shrinking becomes impossible to conceal. Specialists search for the mechanism behind it and attempt treatment, but any improvement is uncertain and temporary. His changing body makes employment and ordinary family roles harder to sustain. Reporters and strangers treat him as a curiosity, adding financial temptation and humiliation to the medical crisis. Louise remains beside him, yet Scott increasingly interprets her help as proof of his dependence. His anger and shame isolate him from the people trying to help.

As Scott becomes exceptionally small, the balance within his home shifts further. Objects, gestures, and even his daughter's growth remind him that the process is continuing. He briefly finds relief in knowing Clarice, a woman whose stature allows him to feel less conspicuous and more nearly equal, but he soon shrinks below even that temporary point of stability. The possibility of a normal adult future recedes, and Scott's fear expresses itself as bitterness toward Louise and toward the life he can no longer occupy on its old terms.

Reduced to only a few inches, Scott is vulnerable inside his own house. A domestic accident and an attack by the family cat separate him from Louise, who concludes that he has been killed. Scott survives but is left in the basement, unable to make himself heard or cross barriers that once meant nothing. The house above effectively disappears from his reach. He begins treating the basement as wilderness, taking stock of water, shelter, tools, and the limited food left within climbing distance.

Scott adapts to solitary survival. He collects drops of water, uses scraps of household material as equipment, and makes exhausting journeys across the basement floor. A piece of cake can sustain him, but a spider occupies the area around it. At his present size the creature is a lethal hunter. Scott studies its movements and prepares a weapon and climbing line, understanding that he must risk a direct confrontation before hunger or continued shrinking leaves him too weak.

Scott reaches the spider's territory and kills it after a prolonged struggle, winning access to food but no rescue from his condition. Still diminishing, he locates a passage through the basement screen and emerges outside. He has long assumed that shrinking to nothing will end his life, yet the expected boundary never arrives. He continues to exist below the scale at which his family could see him. The surrounding world reveals new depths rather than emptiness, and Scott recognizes that size is relative and may extend without a final lower limit. Facing a universe radically larger than the one he knew, he abandons the belief that reduced scale makes his life meaningless and proceeds into the unknown.

characters.description: The Alchemist running the Palm Springs assignment, and by now a working witch in everything but self-description. She has stopped being able to pretend that her magic is a favour to her teacher, and she has stopped being able to pretend that her order tells her the truth. She is still rigidly disciplined, still frightened of what she is becoming, and still living with the memory of turning Adrian down in the cruellest terms available to her.
characters.name: Sydney Sage

characters.description: A royal Moroi spirit user who was told, in the plainest possible language, that a relationship with him is unthinkable. He has not stopped feeling what he feels and has stopped bothering to hide it, which makes every conversation with Sydney an exercise in things neither of them will say. He can walk into other people's dreams, which is both useful and impossible to avoid.
characters.name: Adrian Ivashkov

characters.description: Sydney's history teacher and the witch training her, increasingly urgent about it. She has a sister she does not talk about and a reason for wanting Sydney strong enough to defend herself. Blunt, tired and fond of Sydney in a way she expresses mostly as homework.
characters.name: Jaclyn Terwilliger

characters.description: The Moroi queen's half-sister, still hidden at Amberwood and still the only thing keeping her sister on the throne. The bond with Adrian means she has lived through his heartbreak from the inside, and she knows exactly what Sydney did and why, which she cannot discuss with either of them.
characters.name: Jill Dragomir

characters.description: Jill's dhampir guardian, posing as her brother. Disciplined to a fault and now attached to Angeline, he continues to treat his own feelings as a professional failing.
characters.name: Eddie Castile

characters.description: The dhampir raised among the Keepers, still adjusting badly to human school and still solving problems with her fists. She is with Eddie now, and neither of them is entirely sure it is what they wanted.
characters.name: Angeline Dawes

characters.description: Sydney's lab partner, disowned by the Warriors of Light for helping her. He has lost the future his family planned for him and is working out what is left, while keeping the group's secrets.
characters.name: Trey Juarez

characters.description: Jaclyn Terwilliger's older sister and the reason for her urgency: a witch who takes the magic and the youth of younger witches, leaving them drained and comatose, and who grows stronger with every one she takes. An untrained witch of real power is precisely what she looks for.
characters.name: Veronica Terwilliger

characters.description: A Moroi spirit user and former Strigoi restored by spirit magic, now marrying after years apart from the man she loves. She is one of the few people who can see what Sydney's aura says about her, and she says it kindly.
characters.name: Sonya Karp

characters.description: A Moroi guardian who spent years searching for Sonya while she was Strigoi and who is now marrying her at the Moroi Court.
characters.name: Mikhail Tanner

characters.description: A dhampir guardian to the Moroi queen, blunt and famously reckless, and one of the very few people who has ever seen Sydney break the Alchemists' rules. Their history is the reason Sydney's order has never entirely trusted her.
characters.name: Rose Hathaway

characters.description: The one-eyed self-defence instructor whose lessons Sydney and Adrian keep returning to. His grasp of the world's stranger corners turns out to be better sourced than his manner suggests.
characters.name: Malachi Wolfe

characters.description: An Alchemist who left the order and survived it, now living off the books with a small group of former Alchemists who call themselves the Merry Men. He wears an indigo tattoo over his golden lily and claims to know what the order's tattoos really do to the people who wear them. Charismatic, evasive about his own plans, and very interested in recruiting Sydney.
characters.name: Marcus Finch

characters.description: Sydney's father, a career Alchemist whose marriage is collapsing and who intends to keep his youngest daughter and her career for himself. He regards Sydney's judgement as a liability and does not conceal it.
characters.name: Jared Sage

characters.description: A young witch on the edge of the local coven, apparently weak, apparently harmless and apparently very glad of the help offered to her.
characters.name: Alicia

characters.description: Sydney's younger sister, now committed to the Alchemists and hardened by the choice. She arrives in Palm Springs assigned to the same posting as Sydney, which makes her both family and a witness.
characters.name: Zoe Sage

recaps.ending: Veronica Terwilliger is not the last threat: Alicia, the harmless-seeming young witch on the coven's edge, has been draining witches herself and is the one who finally put Veronica beyond reach. She takes Sydney, intending to take her magic with her, and Sydney destroys her - using power she had spent a year refusing to admit she had, and afterwards being unable to unknow what she is. Sydney goes through with Marcus Finch's procedure and has the compulsion in her golden lily broken, so that she can lie to the Alchemists, refuse them and speak about them without the tattoo stopping her, while still appearing to be an obedient member of the order. She declines to run away with Marcus's group: she will stay inside and keep her people safe. Her family has broken apart in the divorce, and her younger sister Zoe has chosen their father and the Alchemists. Sydney finally admits what she feels and goes to Adrian; they become a couple, with the certainty that discovery would destroy them both. In the last pages Zoe arrives in Palm Springs as Sydney's new Alchemist partner, sent to live beside her and report on everything she does.
recaps.in_short: Sydney is hunting two things at once: Marcus Finch, the Alchemist who escaped the order, and a witch who steals the magic and youth of young witches. The witch is Veronica, Ms. Terwilliger's sister, and Sydney - untrained, powerful and unprotected - is exactly what she looks for. Marcus, found at last, shows Sydney what she half suspects: the golden lily tattoo carries compulsion that keeps Alchemists obedient and silent, and it can be broken. He wants her to run; she wants to stay and protect her people. Meanwhile the search for Veronica runs alongside a Court wedding, a collapsing family and a road trip with Adrian, whose feelings Sydney can no longer honestly deny. When Veronica is finally cornered she has already been drained by someone else: Alicia, a young witch everyone dismissed as harmless, who has been building her own power and now comes for Sydney's. Sydney destroys her with magic she can no longer pretend not to have. She has her tattoo broken, refuses to leave the Alchemists, and chooses Adrian - just as her sister Zoe arrives in Palm Springs to watch her.

recaps.text: Previously: Sydney Sage, an Alchemist, runs the Palm Springs assignment hiding Jill Dragomir, the Moroi queen's half-sister, whose death would cost the queen the throne. Jill attends Amberwood Prep as Sydney's sister, guarded by the dhampirs Eddie Castile and Angeline Dawes, while the royal Moroi Adrian Ivashkov, bonded to Jill since he healed her, lives nearby. Sydney has exposed one corrupt Alchemist, stopped a restored Strigoi who was murdering young Moroi women, and learned that human magic is real: her history teacher Jaclyn Terwilliger is a witch, and Sydney has an unusual gift she was raised to consider abominable. Her friend Trey Juarez turned out to have been raised among the Warriors of Light, a human society that considers every vampire an abomination; when the Warriors captured Sonya Karp - a Moroi who had been Strigoi and was restored - the group rescued her, at the cost of Trey's place among his own people. Afterwards Adrian told Sydney he loved her. She refused him in her order's language, that an Alchemist and a Moroi together is unthinkable, and it devastated him. She has also heard, for the first time, of an Alchemist named Marcus Finch who covered his golden lily with an indigo tattoo and walked away from the order.

Sydney and Adrian are keeping a careful distance that neither of them wants, made harder by his ability to reach her in dreams. Ms. Terwilliger's training turns urgent: young witches in the area are being found drained of their magic and their youth, left comatose, and the woman doing it is her own older sister Veronica. An untrained witch with real power is exactly what Veronica hunts, which makes Sydney a target and makes finishing her training a matter of survival rather than curiosity. At the same time Sydney has not let go of the name Clarence gave her - Marcus Finch, the Alchemist who covered his golden lily and disappeared - because if he got out, the order she has served all her life is not what it claims to be.

The group travels to the Moroi Court for the wedding of Sonya Karp and Mikhail Tanner, where Sydney moves among Moroi royalty as an Alchemist on duty and as a guest, and where she and Adrian spend an evening pretending nothing is happening between them. Court also gives Sydney access to Alchemist business and to people who knew Marcus Finch, and she comes away with a thread to pull. Back in Palm Springs, Ms. Terwilliger pushes her harder, Malachi Wolfe's odd expertise proves useful again, and Sydney begins working the kind of magic she used to insist she was only humouring her teacher by learning. Veronica claims another victim, and the search for her becomes a hunt with a schedule.

Sydney tracks Marcus Finch down. He is living outside the order with a handful of former Alchemists who call themselves the Merry Men, and he tells her what he learned before he ran: the golden lily on every Alchemist's cheek carries compulsion. It is not only a health charm and a seal on their tongues - it makes them loyal, keeps them from questioning orders, and can be reinforced. It can also be broken, by a painful procedure and a second tattoo, which is what the indigo lily over his own is. He wants Sydney to break hers and join him. Sydney, who has spent months noticing what her order does not tell her, believes him, and is not remotely willing to walk away from the people she is responsible for.

The hunt for Veronica takes Sydney and Adrian out on the road together, and the distance they have been keeping does not survive it. Sydney's family is coming apart at the same time: her parents' marriage ends, and Sydney does what she can to keep her younger sister Zoe away from their father and out of the Alchemists, which fails - Zoe chooses him, and holds Sydney's interference against her. Marcus's offer stays open while Sydney puts him off. A young witch called Alicia attaches herself to the coven's edge, apparently frightened and grateful for protection. Veronica's trail leads towards a confrontation Ms. Terwilliger has been dreading for most of her life, and Sydney is the strongest weapon either sister has.

When Sydney and Ms. Terwilliger finally close in on Veronica, they find her already destroyed - drained and left empty by a witch stronger than she was. None of the obvious candidates fit, and the answer, when it comes, is Alicia: the frightened, helpless young witch everyone dismissed, whose weakness was a pose and who has been quietly taking power from every witch who underestimated her. She is stronger now than Veronica ever was, and an untrained talent as large as Sydney's is the prize she has been circling from the start. Sydney has spent the whole hunt being frightened of the wrong woman, and the person who has been closest to her preparations is the one she should have been guarding against.

Alicia takes Sydney, intending to strip her magic the way she stripped Veronica's.
