characters.description: Sarah's father, a prominent judge who recognizes her intelligence but will not permit her to pursue the legal career open to his sons. His affection remains bounded by his commitment to the family's authority and social position.
characters.name: John Faucheraud Grimke

characters.description: Sarah's much younger sister, whom Sarah is allowed to name and promises to guide. Her arrival gives Sarah a chance to encourage in another girl the freedom of judgment that their family has tried to suppress in her.
characters.name: Angelina Grimke

characters.description: A formerly enslaved Charleston carpenter who bought his freedom and becomes a respected leader in the Black community. His opposition to slavery and involvement in organizing offer Handful a vision of collective resistance beyond the private defiance practiced in the Grimke house.
characters.name: Denmark Vesey

characters.description: Handful's younger half-sister, born during the years Charlotte is absent from the Grimke household. Lively and daring, she forms a close alliance with Handful and shares her longing to escape slavery.
characters.name: Sky

characters.description: A widowed Quaker in Philadelphia whose home and religious circle help Sarah imagine a life outside Charleston. His interest in her appears to offer personal companionship as well as a place within the faith she is trying to join.
characters.name: Israel Morris

characters.description: A northern abolitionist organizer and lecturer who works closely with Sarah and Angelina as the antislavery movement expands its public campaign. He supports their controversial decision to address audiences containing both women and men.
characters.name: Theodore Weld

characters.description: The senior enslaved servant in the Grimke household, responsible for much of its daily coordination. He understands both the family's expectations and the quiet networks through which the enslaved residents protect one another.
characters.name: Tomfry

characters.description: A young Charleston man who courts Sarah and appears to offer escape from the isolation created by her ambitions. His conventional assumptions about women eventually expose how limited that escape would be.
characters.name: Burke Williams

recaps.ending: Sarah and Angelina become prominent abolitionist speakers, refusing demands that women remain silent in public reform. Angelina marries fellow abolitionist Theodore Weld, and the sisters continue linking opposition to slavery with women's right to speak and act. In Charleston, Handful has survived the destruction of Denmark Vesey's planned uprising and the executions that followed. Her mother Charlotte, who returned years earlier with Handful's younger sister Sky, is dead, leaving her daughters the story quilt that records her resistance and their family history. Sarah comes back south, outwardly for a family visit but determined to honor her childhood promise. She and Angelina arrange a route out for Handful and Sky. The sisters evade the Grimke household and board a northbound vessel, while Sarah remains behind long enough to protect the escape. Handful leaves Charleston with Sky and with Charlotte's quilt, finally moving toward freedom. Sarah's act cannot undo the decades in which her family owned Handful, but it converts her private conviction into direct aid and closes the long bond between the two women with Handful claiming the future for herself.
recaps.in_short: In 1803 Charleston, eleven-year-old Sarah Grimke is given an enslaved girl, Hetty 'Handful' Grimke, as a birthday present. Sarah tries and fails to free her, then secretly teaches her to read. Over three decades, Handful and her mother Charlotte resist slavery within the Grimke household, while Sarah struggles against the limits placed on wealthy white women and eventually leaves the South for the Quakers and abolitionism. Handful becomes involved in Denmark Vesey's planned uprising; the plot is betrayed, Vesey is executed, and she survives. Charlotte returns after a long absence with another daughter, Sky, and later dies, leaving a quilt that encodes her family story. Sarah and her younger sister Angelina become outspoken antislavery lecturers and defend women's right to speak publicly. Returning to Charleston, Sarah helps Handful and Sky escape by ship. The sisters carry Charlotte's quilt northward, while Sarah remains committed to abolition and women's equality.

recaps.text: In Charleston in 1803, eleven-year-old Sarah Grimke is given ten-year-old Hetty, called Handful, as her personal slave. Sarah writes a document attempting to free her, but her parents reject it and retain ownership. Handful's mother Charlotte, the household seamstress, teaches her daughter that submission need not reach the inner self and begins preserving their history through stories and a quilt. Sarah and Handful form a constrained friendship across the power separating them. Sarah secretly teaches Handful to read, an act forbidden because literacy threatens the system on which the Grimke household rests. When the lessons are discovered, Handful is punished and Sarah retreats under family pressure, leaving both girls marked by the failure of Sarah's first attempt at resistance.

As Sarah grows older, her ambition to study law is dismissed because she is a woman, even while her brothers receive the education she wants. A courtship with Burke Williams briefly seems to offer a different future, but his betrayal and conventional expectations deepen her distrust of marriage as an escape. Sarah's much younger sister Angelina, called Nina, is placed in her care, and Sarah tries to encourage the child's independent conscience. In the work yard, Charlotte continues covert resistance and suffers severe punishment. Handful learns to navigate the household's surveillance while holding onto the reading, stories, and sense of self that she and her mother have protected.

Sarah accompanies her ill father north. After his death she remains in Philadelphia and is drawn to Quaker worship, finding a religious language for the equality she has long believed but also encountering new limits on women's authority. Charlotte, who disappeared from the Grimke household years earlier, returns with Handful's younger half-sister Sky. Her health has been broken by violence and hardship, and she dies after reuniting with her daughter, leaving behind the quilt through which she preserved family memory and dreams of freedom. Sarah's physical distance from slavery does not resolve her responsibility for the person legally attached to her name.

Handful becomes involved in the dangerous preparations around Denmark Vesey's planned uprising, carrying forward the resistance Charlotte taught her. The conspiracy is betrayed before it can begin. Charleston authorities arrest Black leaders, use fear and testimony to widen the prosecutions, and execute Vesey and others. Handful survives without surrendering the desire for freedom, but the crackdown devastates the community. In the North, Sarah's hopes for a settled Quaker life, including her attachment to the widower Israel Morris, collapse when she recognizes that the role offered to her still requires submission of her public purpose.

Handful and Sky preserve the quilt through which Charlotte recorded ancestry, suffering, and resistance, understanding it as both family memory and a guide toward freedom. Sarah and Nina commit themselves more openly to abolition. Their writings and public speaking attract support but also hostility, especially because they address audiences containing men and claim women's authority to participate in political and religious debate. Pressure from family, clergy, and former Quaker allies does not silence them. The sisters' campaign makes Sarah's long opposition to slavery public, but she still carries the unresolved promise she made to Handful in childhood.

Angelina marries abolitionist Theodore Weld, and she and Sarah continue speaking and writing against slavery while also defending women's public equality. Sarah returns to Charleston with a concealed purpose: to help Handful leave the family that has held her for most of her life. With Angelina's assistance she arranges passage and creates the opportunity for Handful and Sky to get away. The two women evade the household and reach a northbound ship carrying Charlotte's story quilt. Sarah cannot erase her family's ownership or the unequal conditions of her bond with Handful, but she finally acts directly on the freedom document she tried to write as a child. Handful and Sky sail out of Charleston toward the North, preserving their mother's history and claiming an uncertain life beyond slavery for themselves.
